analysis.one_liner: Lets survivors of sexual harassment and assault speak publicly despite pre-dispute NDAs.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the Senate unanimously, passed the House 315-109, and was signed into law on December 7, 2022 (Public Law 117-224).
analysis.plain_summary: Companies often make workers, contractors, and customers sign agreements years in advance saying they will never publicly discuss sexual misconduct. This law says courts cannot enforce those pre-existing silence clauses when the dispute involves sexual assault or sexual harassment that may have broken federal, state, or tribal law. It does not stop someone from signing a settlement with confidentiality terms after a dispute is known.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, independent contractors, and consumers who signed a nondisclosure or nondisparagement agreement before a dispute arose, and who are later involved in a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute: courts can no longer enforce those clauses against them, so they can report and publicly discuss the misconduct [S7]. Congress's own findings note that an estimated 87 to 94 percent of people who experience workplace sexual harassment never file a formal complaint, and that silencing clauses shield perpetrators and let abuse continue [S7].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Harassment and assault survivors bound by pre-dispute NDAs

how_it_helps.text: With respect to a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute, no nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause agreed to before the dispute arises can be judicially enforced when the alleged conduct may violate federal, tribal, or state law [S7].

Congress found that nondisclosure and nondisparagement provisions between employers and employees, and between providers of goods and services and consumers, can perpetuate illegal conduct by silencing survivors while shielding perpetrators and enabling them to continue their abuse [S7].
The law preserves stronger state protections, does not touch pseudonym rules that let victims sue anonymously, and explicitly leaves trade secrets and proprietary information protected [S7].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and other parties who relied on pre-dispute NDAs and nondisparagement clauses lose a tool for keeping sexual misconduct disputes out of public view; companies face more public exposure of harassment and assault allegations, and perpetrators lose a contractual shield [S7]. Employers retain the right to protect trade secrets and proprietary information [S7].

drawbacks.text: The law covers only clauses signed before a dispute arises. Post-dispute settlement agreements with confidentiality terms — the kind most people associate with high-profile harassment settlements — remain enforceable, so many settlements that silence accusers are unaffected [S7].

It applies only to sexual assault and sexual harassment disputes, not to discrimination based on race, disability, wage theft, or other misconduct, and it does not ban mandatory arbitration itself, which can still keep claims out of court [S7].

Employers objected that the bill was rushed to a floor vote closed to amendments with only one hour of debate; in the House, 109 of 213 Republicans voted no, more than the 100 who voted yes [S9] [S10].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly restores the ability of millions of workers and consumers to speak about sexual assault and harassment, addressing conduct Congress found affects 81 percent of women and 43 percent of men over their lifetimes. Its honest limitation is scope: because it reaches only pre-dispute clauses, the settlement NDAs that receive the most public attention remain untouched, and other forms of workplace misconduct are not covered. It is a real but partial protection [S7].

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate without any senator objecting, passed the House 315-109, and the President signed it into law on December 7, 2022.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Gillibrand on July 13, 2022, with 14 cosponsors including 5 Republicans, and was referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1] [S9].
The Judiciary Committee reported the bill favorably on September 20, 2022, and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent on September 29, 2022 — meaning no senator demanded a recorded vote [S9].
The House passed it on November 16, 2022, 315-109, with 215 of 219 voting Democrats in favor and Republicans split 100 yes to 109 no [S10] [S9].
President Biden signed it on December 7, 2022, and it became Public Law 117-224 [S9] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Survivors of sexual assault and harassment are better off because they can no longer be blocked from speaking by contracts they signed before knowing of any dispute. Employers and perpetrators who used those clauses to keep misconduct quiet lost that shield.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Harassment survivors; employers lost an NDA shield

against.what_they_did: The bill came to the floor under a rule allowing one hour of debate with no amendments, and the 109 no votes were the only recorded opposition in either chamber.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate passed it with no recorded opposition, but the House split largely by party: 215 of 219 Democrats voted yes while Republicans divided 100 yes to 109 no.

industries.industry: Employers (large and small businesses that use NDAs)
industries.note: Pre-dispute nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses in employment agreements can no longer be enforced in sexual assault or harassment disputes, so employers lose a tool for keeping such allegations out of public view. They retain trade-secret and proprietary-information protections, and post-dispute settlement NDAs still work [S7].

industries.industry: Providers of goods and services (businesses that make customers sign NDAs)
industries.note: Congress's findings singled out agreements between providers of goods or services and consumers, which can no longer silence consumers in sexual misconduct disputes [S7].
